title: The Eagle’s Nest, a Nazi icon, just burned. Should Germany rebuild it?
text:
The Eagle’s Nest, a Nazi icon, just burned. Should Germany rebuild it?
Germans once again have to decide what they should do with Nazi-era relics after a fire destroyed the Bavarian guest house linked to Adolf Hitler.
An arsonist has once again hurled Germany into a question that it has spent more than 80 years answering: What should it do with the architectural relics of the Nazi regime?
Authorities in the southern state of Bavaria have arrested a man in connection with the wholesale destruction of the Eagle’s Nest, a Nazi guest house visited several times by Adolf Hitler. Its stunning location atop a peak with sweeping views of the Alps made it the backdrop for Nazi propaganda films and, more recently, a significant tourist attraction.
Investigators have not yet offered a motive but pointed to the suspect’s record of mental illness.
Architectural relics from the Nazi era can help people draw lessons from the past. Some, such as the Eagle’s Nest guest house frequented by Hitler, also draw large numbers of tourists. But after its destruction in a fire, Germans are having to decide whether the mountaintop retreat should be rebuilt.
In the hours after the fire, Bavaria’s interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, considered what might come next. “We can hardly leave a ruin standing there,” he said at a news conference, suggesting the structure would be rebuilt.
In many ways, it was the same dilemma faced by the German city of Nuremberg, where the Nazi Parade Grounds and Congress Hall were falling into ruin. Or by the Austrian town of Braunau am Inn, where no one knew quite what to do with Hitler’s birthplace.
Nuremberg has chosen to renovate its Nazi past, both to keep the lessons of the past fresh, but also to give historic structures a new story. The massive Congress Hall is being renovated as a space for art and theater. Hitler’s birthplace in Austria became a police station.
But preservation and restoration have not always been the default. Almost nothing of the Berlin Wall remains, with locals having to step in to save a few short sections and watchtowers. And the German government razed Hitler’s war bunkers in Berlin after World War II, worried they might become a place of pilgrimage for white supremacists. The last remnants of that complex are now set to be demolished to make way for an apartment block. One tourist operator called the plan “absolute madness,” saying Berlin shouldn’t run away from its history, according to The Spectator.
Now, Germany has a new decision to make with the Eagle’s Nest.
“For many, Germany has become a model for dealing with the legacies of dictatorship, war, and genocide,” says Gerald Steinacher, an expert on Nazi Germany at the University of Nebraska, in an email interview. “Still, how best to deal with Nazi buildings and sites remains an ongoing struggle.”
